title: Open Loop vs. Closed Loop
question: Can we just *tell* the drone what thrust to use?

blocks.text: I borrowed a drone! Its job: carry small packages and **hover at exactly 2 metres** so someone can grab them.
It's like the shower, right? One number we want (2 m), one thing we can change (how hard the propellers push).

Here are the facts. The drone weighs **0.5 kg**, so gravity pulls it down with $0.5 \times 9.81 \approx 4.9$ newtons. The propellers push up with a {eff|thrust} $\eff{T}$ that we choose. When the drone moves, air pushes back a little: about **1 newton for every metre per second** of speed.

Don't worry about the dots over the $\out{h}$ yet. They mean "how fast $\out{h}$ is changing" and we'll build them properly in Chapter 3. For now, the idea in words: **push harder than 4.9 N and you speed up going up; push less and you speed up going down.** Push exactly 4.9 N and you keep doing whatever you were already doing.

Honest simplifications: our drone only moves up and down, air drag is a neat straight-line rule, and for the next few chapters the motors have unlimited power (they can even pull down a little). Real drones are messier. We'll add the mess back later.

sections.title: Just tell it what to do

blocks.text: We know the physics exactly. So we don't need to *look* at anything. We can **calculate** a plan: push hard for a bit to climb, then push exactly 4.9 N to hover.
That kind of plan is called **open loop**: the plan decides the thrust, and nobody checks what actually happens. Try it. Choose a climb thrust and how long to climb, then launch.

I worked it out. While climbing, the drone soon settles into a steady speed of (extra thrust ÷ drag). The height you end up at is just **(extra thrust ÷ drag) × climb time**. For 6 N that's $(6 - 4.9)/1 \approx 1.1$ m/s, so climb for $2 \div 1.1 \approx 1.83$ seconds.
Press **Theo's plan**. It lands on 2.00 m. Beautiful.
Theo, that's amazing! We're done! Chapter over!
Let's just check what happens outside… there's a bit of a breeze today.
Run Theo's plan again, and while it's hovering press **Gust** (a push downward of 1 N for one second).
It dropped about a metre… and it's **staying** down there. My numbers were right!
Your numbers were perfect. The wind just wasn't in your plan. And the drone has no idea it's in the wrong place.

That was our mistake: we believed **"if you get the numbers right, you don't need feedback."** The calm-air success was real, and the plan was still useless the moment the world did something it didn't expect. After the gust, the thrust is exactly 4.9 N again, so the drone just stays wherever the gust left it.
Now the real job. Below, the drone is hovering at 2 m with a fixed 4.9 N of thrust, exactly balancing its weight. Someone clips on a **0.2 kg package**.

blocks.q: The package makes the drone heavier, but the thrust stays at 4.9 N. What happens?

options.text: It sinks a little, then stops
options.why: It feels like the drone should find a new balance. But at a steady 4.9 N it's too heavy at *every* height: nothing about being lower helps it.

options.text: It sinks and keeps sinking, all the way down
options.why: The extra 2 N of weight is never balanced. Drag stops it speeding up past about **2 m/s**, but it keeps falling at that speed until it hits the ground.

options.text: Nothing: 0.2 kg is too small to matter
options.why: Any mismatch between thrust and weight makes it drift. 0.2 kg adds about 2 N, which is big compared with the drag.

blocks.text: **Crash.** Nothing in an open-loop plan can notice that the drone is falling. Now switch the mode to **Feedback: look at the height**, reset, and try the package and the gust again.
In feedback mode the drone uses a simple rule: **push with the hover thrust, plus an extra 8 N for every metre it is too low.**
Whoa. The gust knocks it down less than 20 cm, and it climbs right back. The package makes it dip, but it doesn't crash!
It doesn't need to know *what* happened. It just sees it's too low and pushes harder. That's the trick.
But look: with the package it settles at about **1.75 m**, not 2. Why doesn't it go all the way back?
Keep June's question in your pocket. It's the whole of Chapter 2.
Engineers draw these systems as boxes and arrows called **block diagrams**. Each box does something; each arrow carries a signal. We drew ours on the whiteboard one piece at a time.

The key difference is that one arrow, looping back from the output to the start. That's why feedback control is called **closed loop**: information goes all the way round. Scroll back up to the package test: the diagram under the drone lights up whichever part is busy right now.

items.def: What we want: 2 m of height, 38 °C of water.
What actually happens: the real height.
How far off we are. Positive means too low.
The rule that turns the error into an action. So far: "8 N extra per metre too low."
What the controller actually does: the thrust.
The thing being controlled: the drone itself, physics and all. (An odd word, from old factory "plants".)
Whatever measures the output: the drone's height sensor, your skin in the shower.
Anything the world does that we didn't plan for: gusts, packages, someone flushing a toilet.
Acting from a plan without looking / acting on what you measure.

blocks.text: Here's the same diagram for a car's **cruise control**. The setpoint is a speed, the plant is the car, and the disturbance is a hill. The controller presses the accelerator harder when the car is slower than it should be.
Thermostats, cruise control, the shower, our drone… it's the **same loop** every time, with different labels!

items: **Open loop** means following a plan without looking. It can be perfect in calm conditions and useless the moment something unexpected happens.
**Closed loop (feedback)** means measuring the output, comparing it with the setpoint (the **error**), and acting on that.
Feedback handles disturbances it has never heard of: gusts, packages, anything.
Block diagrams show the loop: setpoint → error → controller → plant → output → sensor → back again.
Our simple feedback rule stopped the crash, but with the package it settled about 25 cm low. Why?

items.q: In the shower from Chapter 0, what plays the role of the **sensor**?

options.why: The knob is how you *act*: it sets the control effort. It doesn't measure anything.
Yes. Your skin measures the output (the water temperature) and feeds it back to the controller (your brain).
The pipe is part of the **plant**, the thing being controlled. It's where the delay comes from.

items.q: Which of these is a **closed-loop** system?

options.why: The timer doesn't check how brown the toast is. It just follows the plan: open loop.
Right. It measures the room temperature and switches the heating on or off based on the error.

options.text: A washing machine running a fixed programme
options.why: It follows its programme regardless of how dirty the clothes are: open loop.

items.q: The setpoint is 2 m and the drone is at 1.5 m. What is the error $\err{e} = \sp{r} - \out{h}$, and what should the controller do?

options.why: Positive error means too low, so more thrust. With our rule that's $4.9 + 8 \times 0.5 = 8.9$ N.
Check the order: $\sp{r} - \out{h} = 2 - 1.5 = +0.5$. We pick this sign convention so that positive error means "too low".
The error is a *difference*, not a sum: $2 - 1.5 = 0.5$ m.

blocks.text: Our loop has a mystery number in it: **8 newtons per metre**. Why 8? Why not 2, or 50? And why does the drone settle too low?

d.aria: Block diagram of the drone's control loop
d.description: Target minus measured height gives the error; the controller turns the error into thrust; thrust and disturbances act on the drone; the drone's height is measured by the sensor and fed back to be subtracted from the target. In open-loop mode only the forward path is shown.

whiteboard.title: Drawing the loop, one piece at a time
whiteboard.step1: Mika: "Thrust goes in, height comes out. The drone is a box that turns one into the other." We call it the plant.
whiteboard.step2: Theo: "Open loop: we pick the thrust from a plan, based only on the target."
whiteboard.step3: June: "And the world pushes on the drone too: wind, packages. Disturbances."
whiteboard.step4: Mika: "So let's measure the height with a sensor…"
whiteboard.step5: Theo: "…and subtract it from the target. That difference is the error, and the controller acts on it. The loop is closed!"

d.aria: Block diagram being drawn step by step
d.description: A block diagram built in five steps: the plant alone; an open-loop plan feeding it; disturbances acting on it; a sensor measuring the output; and finally the error, controller and summing junction closing the loop.

d.aria: Block diagram of a car's cruise control
d.description: Target speed minus measured speed gives the speed error; the cruise controller turns it into accelerator pedal; the pedal and hills act on the car; the speedometer measures the speed and feeds it back.
